title: Run a wick lamp or hurricane lantern
summary: A wick lamp burns clear K-1 kerosene or lamp oil drawn up a cotton wick, and gives a dim light for many hours on a cupful or so of fuel. Petrol, camp fuel or alcohol in one can explode; filled hot, tipped or left burning, it starts fires; and like every flame it uses room air and makes carbon monoxide. A hurricane lantern is an outdoor light unless its maker says otherwise.

materials.item: Wick lamp or hurricane lantern with a sound glass chimney or globe
Clear K-1 kerosene or clear, unscented lamp oil
materials.qty: about 300 mL (10 US fl oz) per fill for a small lantern

materials.item: Spare cotton wick of the burner's width
Small funnel, metal tray and rags for filling
Pie pan or other flat metal lid to smother a flare-up
Battery CO alarm and smoke alarm in the room

steps.text: Read the lamp's label or manual first, and treat a hurricane (storm) lantern as an outdoor light unless its own manual says it is made for indoor use. Feuerhand's Baby Special 276 manual says outdoors only and rules out use in households, residential buildings and any other rooms, in sheds and huts, and in tents (Feuerhand 276). Health Canada says not to use oil lamps in enclosed areas unless they are specifically designed for indoor use (Health Canada CO). Aladdin's safety page tells you how to run its mantle lamps in a ventilated room, with wide clearances (Aladdin safety), and Be Ready Utah treats oil lamps rated indoor safe as emergency lights for a well-ventilated room (Be Ready Utah lamps). Pressure lanterns are a different machine; see [Liquid-fuel stoves](#guides/skill_liquid_fuel_stove).

Use only clear K-1 kerosene or clear, unscented lamp oil (Aladdin safety, Aladdin FAQ, Feuerhand 276). No coloured or scented oils, which gum the wick (Feuerhand 276, Lanternnet care), and no thick paraffin oil in wide wicks (Aladdin FAQ).
steps.warn: Never petrol, camp fuel (white gas), naphtha, alcohol, paint thinner or diesel in a wick lamp (Aladdin safety, Feuerhand 276, Lanternnet fuels). Petrol gives off burnable vapour at −43 °C (NIOSH petrol).

steps.text: Fill it out and cold: outdoors, or over a metal tray, away from any flame and away from children. Fill only to the mark or shoulder, not the brim: Feuerhand says about 300 mL in its 340 mL tank (Feuerhand 276). Wipe up spills at once, cap the fuel and lock it away (Be Ready Utah lamps, [Lamp oil and children](#guides/safety_lamp_oil_children)).
steps.warn: Never refill a lamp that is lit or still hot (Aladdin safety, Feuerhand 276, Be Ready Utah lamps).

steps.text: A new or dry wick needs time to soak up fuel before you light it: about 20 minutes says Feuerhand (Feuerhand 276), an hour says Be Ready Utah (Be Ready Utah lamps).

Trim the wick: cut off the black, burnt top straight across with sharp scissors, neatly and without fraying (Feuerhand 276, Lanternnet care). Nipping each corner off at 45° is an old trick for a rounder flame (Cottage Life lamps). A flame with peaks and dips means it needs trimming again (Cottage Life lamps).

Set the lamp on a level, steady surface that won't burn, out of reach of children and pets and out of draughts (Aladdin safety, Health Canada oil lamps). Keep anything that burns at least 45 cm (18 in) around and 90 cm (36 in) above the chimney, the figures Aladdin gives for its lamps (Aladdin safety).
steps.warn: The top of an Aladdin chimney runs above 537 °C (1,000 °F) (Aladdin safety).

steps.text: Light it: raise the globe or take off the chimney, wind the wick up just above the burner (Feuerhand says 1–2 mm), light it, and put the glass back gently (Feuerhand 276). Start with a smaller flame than you want, because it grows as the lamp warms (Lanternnet care). A lamp that has been out in the cold needs to come up to room temperature before you light it (Aladdin safety); for a lantern you will use in freezing weather, Lanternnet says to light it outside to avoid breaking the globe (Lanternnet care). On an Aladdin, wait 20 minutes before turning it up (Aladdin safety).
steps.warn: Turning a mantle lamp up too fast can crack the chimney or make it run away (Aladdin safety).

steps.text: Set the flame: steady, not flickering, no soot. Feuerhand gives 1.5–2 cm for its lantern (Feuerhand 276). A flame that smokes or soots is burning incompletely (Lanternnet fuels), and Feuerhand says the flame should not flicker or soot (Feuerhand 276). Turn it down, trim the wick and check you have the right fuel in it.

Give it air: a cracked window in a tight room (Aladdin safety, Be Ready Utah lamps), and a CO alarm in the room. Lanterns are among the fuel burners that make carbon monoxide (CDC CO). A lamp that dims after an hour or two may be short of air (Aladdin FAQ).
steps.warn: Never burn a lamp in a tent, a closed vehicle or the blanket den you sleep in (CPSC camping, Feuerhand 276); see [Candles](#guides/safety_candles).

steps.text: Don't carry a lamp lit, and don't tilt, swing or move a filled lantern: it leaks (Feuerhand 276). Lift a lamp by its font or base, never the burner (Aladdin safety); on a lantern touch only the bail handle (Feuerhand 276).

Put it out before you sleep or leave the room (Aladdin safety, Be Ready Utah lamps). On a lantern, wind the wick down until the flame dies, then turn it up a little to check it is out, without winding it so far it drops out of the burner (Feuerhand 276).

When it's cold, clean the glass: soapy water, or rub it with crumpled newspaper (Cottage Life lamps, Feuerhand 276). Brush char off the wick, and check the glass for cracks and chips (Lanternnet care).
To store or move a lantern, empty the fuel out first and keep it somewhere dry (Feuerhand 276). Fuel goes back in its labelled can, locked away.

notes:
## Which lamp is which

| Lamp | How it works | Indoors? |
|---|---|---|
| Flat-wick table lamp | A flat cotton wick in a brass burner, glass chimney on top | Made for it, with ventilation (Be Ready Utah lamps) |
| Hurricane (storm) lantern: Dietz, Feuerhand | Flat wick inside a wire-guarded globe; tubes feed it air | Outdoors, unless the maker's manual says otherwise: Feuerhand's 276 manual forbids use in homes, other rooms, sheds and tents (Feuerhand 276) |
| Centre-draft mantle lamp: Aladdin | Round wick heats a mantle that glows | Yes, ventilated, with wide clearances (Aladdin safety) |
| Pressure lantern: Coleman, Petromax | Pumped fuel through a generator to a mantle | Outdoor use; see [Liquid-fuel stoves](#guides/skill_liquid_fuel_stove) and the lantern device card |

Propane and white-gas lanterns are for outdoor use only because of the gases they give off (Be Ready Utah lamps). The [Fuel lantern](#browse/devices/fuel_lantern) card lists fuel lanterns as outdoor only; for any wick lamp or lantern, the maker's label or manual says where it can be used.

## Fuel: what's safe in a wick

| Fuel | Flash point | In a wick lamp |
|---|---|---|
| Petrol (gasoline) | −43 °C (−45 °F) (NIOSH petrol) | Never: it gives off burnable vapour even in the cold |
| Kerosene | 38–72 °C (100–162 °F) (NIOSH kerosene) | Yes, clear K-1, if the lamp's maker names it (Aladdin safety); Lanternnet lists plain kerosene as an outdoor-only fuel because of its smell (Lanternnet fuels) |
| Lamp oil (refined kerosene) | Aladdin's own: 61 °C (141 °F) (Lanternnet fuels) | Yes: clear and unscented (Feuerhand 276, Be Ready Utah lamps) |
| Canola cooking oil | 275–290 °C (OSU canola) | Not in a lamp: too thick for the wick (Lanternnet fuels) |

The flash point is roughly the lowest temperature at which the fuel gives off enough vapour to catch. The higher it is, the more forgiving the fuel. Lamp oil is kerosene with most of the sulphur taken out, which is why it smells less (Lanternnet fuels). Straight kerosene has an odour and will smoke a little (Aladdin FAQ). A lamp that keeps smelling strongly is letting unburned fuel escape; stop using it until you find out why (Lanternnet fuels).

Names get confusing. In North America, paraffin lamp oil is a thicker, purer oil that suits small wicks only; it is too thick for wicks 7/8 in (22 mm) or wider (Lanternnet care, Aladdin FAQ), and Lanternnet says it cuts the light by about half (Lanternnet care). Read what the lamp's maker asks for.

Coloured and scented oils clog wicks (Lanternnet care, Cottage Life lamps), and they are exactly the bottles children mistake for juice; see [Lamp oil and children](#guides/safety_lamp_oil_children).

## The wick and the flame

- The wick only carries fuel up to the flame; it isn't meant to burn away. A thin black char on top is normal, and crumbling char needs brushing off (Lanternnet fuels).
- Running a lamp dry shortens the wick's life: keep it above a quarter full (Lanternnet fuels). Be Ready Utah says keep it three-quarters full (Be Ready Utah lamps).
- Set the flame a little lower than you want and let the lamp warm up: the flame burns higher once the lantern reaches operating temperature (Lanternnet care), and Aladdin says to wait 20 minutes before turning a mantle lamp up (Aladdin safety). Soot means incomplete burning (Lanternnet fuels).
- Wide wicks need thin fuel. Thick oils can't climb a large wick (Aladdin FAQ).

## The chimney glass

The glass draws air past the flame and keeps draughts off it, so the lamp only burns cleanly with the glass on: Aladdin says its chimney must always be in place while lit (Aladdin safety). It gets very hot. Turning a lamp up too fast can crack it (Aladdin safety). Wash off soot when the glass is cold (Feuerhand 276, Cottage Life lamps), and keep a spare: a cracked chimney goes in the scrap.

## How much light, honestly

- Researchers in an off-grid African night market measured two kerosene hurricane lanterns at 1.9 and 5 lux at 1 m. They give unpressurised wick lamps and candles as under 5 lux at 1 m, and a pressurised kerosene lamp as 50 to 75 lux (LBNL illuminance).
- The vendors they surveyed put the least acceptable light at about 2 lux. The note's review of other studies gives 5–15 lux for general home lighting and 25 lux or more for reading (LBNL illuminance). By those figures a hurricane lantern is enough to move about and do a simple task close to it, and well short of reading light.
- Aladdin says its mantle lamp gives about as much light as six flat-wick lamps combined (Aladdin FAQ): a maker's claim, not a measurement.
- On the plus side, a Feuerhand 276 holds 340 mL and burns about 20 hours (Feuerhand 276): roughly 17 mL (half a US fl oz) an hour.

A small LED lamp beats all of them on light and on fire risk; burn fuel when the batteries are gone.

## Air and carbon monoxide

Lanterns are on CDC's list of fuel burners that make carbon monoxide (CDC CO). Soot on the glass is a sign of incomplete burning (Lanternnet fuels), and CO builds up when fuel burns short of air. Ventilate (Aladdin safety, Be Ready Utah lamps), keep a battery CO alarm in the room, and never burn a lamp where you sleep. See [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## Improvised wicks and cooking-oil lamps

- **Wicks.** Candle wicks are braided or twisted fabric, usually cotton (NIST candles), and Lanternnet sells lamp wicks of pure cotton (Lanternnet fuels). The wick only carries fuel, so a strip of plain, undyed cotton cloth cut to the burner's width may stand in for a lost one. No source opened tests this, so watch it closely for smoke and a high flame. Nylon, polyester and polypropylene melt in flame (see [Open flames](#browse/hazards/open_flame)), so check the fibre. Soak it before lighting, as with a new wick.
- **Cooking oil.** Fresh canola oil has an open-cup flash point of 275–290 °C and a viscosity of 78 mm²/s at 20 °C (OSU canola). That makes it slow to catch, which helps, but too thick to climb a lamp's long wick, so don't pour it into a kerosene lamp (Lanternnet fuels). Home-made dish lamps burning cooking oil are not covered by any fire-safety source opened for this card, so treat one as an untested open flame.
- Hard to light doesn't mean safe. A dish of hot, burning cooking oil is a grease fire: cover it with a lid and never use water (see [Common fires](#ref/reference_fire_heat/common_fires)). Treat any home-made lamp exactly like a candle: on a metal tray, nothing above, never unattended ([Candles](#guides/safety_candles)).

## When it goes wrong

- **Flame climbing or flaring out of the chimney (a runaway, usually a mantle lamp):** wind the wick all the way down at once, or cover the top of the chimney with a pie pan or other flat, non-burning lid. If that doesn't work, wrap a damp rag round the air holes in the burner (Aladdin safety). Don't pick it up.
- **Wrong fuel by mistake:** don't light it. Empty it outdoors once it is cold, and fit a new wick before you use it again (Aladdin safety).
- **Spilled fuel burning:** treat it as a fuel fire: smother it, no water ([Fuel](#browse/hazards/fuel)). If it spreads, get out and close the door; see [When no help is coming](#ref/safety_candles/when_no_help_is_coming).
- **Headache, dizziness or nausea with a lamp burning:** put it out, get into fresh air, and read [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).
